Agentic artificial intelligence is rapidly emerging as a paradigm in which large language models, retrieval systems, memory modules, software tools, and multi-agent coordination mechanisms are integrated to support autonomous or semi-autonomous decision-making. Unlike conventional AI systems that primarily produce predictions or responses, agentic AI systems can interpret goals, decompose tasks, retrieve external evidence, invoke tools, interact with digital environments, communicate with other agents, and execute multi-step workflows. These capabilities introduce trustworthiness challenges because failures may propagate from generated text into planning, tool calls, workflow execution, external communication, and real-world decision support. This paper presents a rapid, PRISMA-informed evidence review of trustworthy agentic AI across a primary corpus of 33 studies, complemented by one additional structural reference used only to model manuscript organization, focusing on safety, explainability, alignment, human oversight, fairness, privacy, security, evaluation, and governance. The review reports transparent search and screening procedures, a seven-item quality assessment applied to every primary study, and quantitative synthesis of publication trends, source types, and trust-dimension coverage. Agentic artificial intelligence is rapidly emerging as a paradigm in which large language models, retrieval systems, memory modules, software tools, and multi-agent coordination mechanisms are integrated to support autonomous or semi-autonomous decision-making. Unlike conventional AI systems that primarily produce predictions or responses, agentic AI systems can interpret goals, decompose tasks, retrieve external evidence, invoke tools, interact with digital environments, communicate with other agents, and execute multi-step workflows. These capabilities introduce trustworthiness challenges because failures may propagate from generated text into planning, tool calls, workflow execution, external communication, and real-world decision support. This paper presents a rapid, PRISMA-informed evidence review of trustworthy agentic AI across a primary corpus of 33 studies, complemented by one additional structural reference used only to model manuscript organization, focusing on safety, explainability, alignment, human oversight, fairness, privacy, security, evaluation, and governance. The review reports transparent search and screening procedures, a seven-item quality assessment applied to every primary study, and quantitative synthesis of publication trends, source types, and trust-dimension coverage. The paper proposes the T-SAFE taxonomy, organizing trustworthy agentic AI around Transparency, Safety, Alignment, Fairness, and Explainability, and introduces a layered trustworthy agentic AI framework linking environment interaction, memory, retrieval, tool use, reasoning, trust controls, governance, and human oversight. The taxonomy is explicitly positioned against fifteen related academic, industry, and regulatory frameworks published between 2023 and 2026, including four closely related systematic surveys published in 2026, to clarify its specific contribution. 3.7 Manuscript type considerations
Given the rapid-review methodology disclosed in Sect.
3.5
, this manuscript is positioned as a review article presenting a rapid evidence review together with a novel taxonomy and architectural framework contribution, rather than as a claim of methodological equivalence to exhaustive multi-database systematic literature reviews. Authors submitting this manuscript type are encouraged to confirm manuscript-type classification and fit with the handling editor prior to or during submission, and to reference this section if the distinction is raised during peer review.
The primary evidence base comprises 33 unique studies retained after screening, duplicate removal, and separation of the structural reference described in Sect.
3.6
(one duplicate record, an earlier double-count of the same evaluation survey, was also identified and removed during reference consolidation). Table
4
reports the composition of this corpus by source type, and Table
5
reports its distribution by publication year, both computed directly from the 33 primary studies in the final reference list, excluding the structural reference.

Two findings from Tables
4
and
5
are directly relevant to the review’s motivation and threats to validity. First, 73% of the primary corpus was published in 2025 or 2026, confirming the rapid recency of this literature and reinforcing why a review completed via exhaustive multi-database export would risk being outdated before publication — a practical trade-off explicitly weighed in Sect.
9
. Second, arXiv preprints constitute the largest single category (42%), which is expected given publication lag in this fast-moving subfield, but which also motivates the quality assessment reported in Sect.
5.4
, since preprint status alone does not indicate methodological rigor.
5.1 Agentic AI architecture patterns
Modern agentic AI systems are composed of multiple interacting components, including LLM reasoning controllers, memory modules, retrieval systems, tools, APIs, web environments, human feedback channels, and other agents (Wang et al. 2023; Luo et al.
2025
; Minaee et al. 2024). Multi-agent architectures extend this design through role specialization, debate, and inter-agent communication (Guo et al.
2024
), while WebAgents extend it into direct web navigation and transaction execution (Ning et al.
2025
). Each component introduces trustworthiness risks that must be evaluated separately and jointly (Table
6
).

Agentic AI architecture patterns
Architecture pattern
Description
Trustworthiness concern
LLM-based single agent
An LLM controls task interpretation, planning, and response generation.
Hallucinated reasoning, weak self-correction, and overconfidence.
Tool-augmented agent
The agent invokes APIs, software tools, databases, code execution, or workflows.
Unsafe tool calls, unauthorized execution, and irreversible actions.
RAG-enabled agent
The agent retrieves external content before reasoning or acting.
Prompt injection, source poisoning, stale knowledge, and irrelevant retrieval.
Multi-agent system
Multiple specialized agents collaborate, debate, verify, or coordinate.
Cascading errors, role ambiguity, conflicting goals, and accountability gaps.

The agent navigates websites and executes instructions in web settings.
